title: Amos 3:1–8
context: Amos addresses the whole family the LORD brought up from Egypt. The LORD says he has chosen only them of all the families of the earth, and therefore he will punish them for all their sins. Amos then poses a series of questions about cause and effect (two walking together, a lion roaring, a bird in a snare, a trumpet in a city, and calamity in a city) leading to his conclusion: the Lord GOD reveals his plans to the prophets, and when he has spoken, the prophet cannot keep silent. Shared ground: privilege brings accountability, and God’s word compels the prophet to speak.

verses.text: Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up out of the land of Egypt, saying:
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos calls Israel to hear the word the LORD has spoken against the whole family he brought up from Egypt. Arminian readers see covenant history as the setting for accountability.

The address includes all the tribes.
verses.reformedNotes:
“The whole family” may include Judah as well as Israel.

Reformed readers see God addressing the people he redeemed. Shared ground: both traditions read the exodus as the ground of Israel’s relationship and responsibility.

verses.text: “I have chosen only you of all the families of the earth. Therefore I will punish you for all of your sins.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I have chosen only you of all the families of the earth. Therefore I will punish you for all of your sins.”

Arminian readers see covenant election bringing responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s free choice of Israel heightening, not lessening, its accountability.

See Deuteronomy 7:7 for how each tradition reads Israel’s election. Shared ground: privilege brings greater accountability, not exemption.

verses.text: Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos asks, “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” A series of questions begins. Arminian readers see cause and effect linking events.

The questions build toward the prophet’s message.
verses.reformedNotes:
Each question expects the answer no, leading the hearer to accept the next step.

Reformed readers see logic pointing to God as the cause behind the prophetic word. Shared ground: both traditions read the questions as arguing that nothing happens without a cause.

verses.text: Will a lion roar in the thicket, when he has no prey? Does a young lion cry out of his den, if he has caught nothing?
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos asks whether a lion roars in the thicket without prey, or a young lion cries from its den if it has caught nothing. Arminian readers see a warning in the lion image.

The roar signals that something is happening.
verses.reformedNotes:
The lion image recalls 1:2, where the LORD roars from Zion.

Reformed readers see God’s roar as a sign of coming judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the lion as a picture of the LORD’s warning voice.

verses.text: Can a bird fall in a trap on the earth, where no snare is set for him? Does a snare spring up from the ground, when there is nothing to catch?
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos asks whether a bird falls into a trap where no snare is set, or a snare springs up when nothing is caught. Arminian readers see consequences as connected to causes.

The imagery continues the series.
verses.reformedNotes:
The trap imagery may suggest that Israel is already caught in the consequences of its sin.

Reformed readers see God’s purposes at work behind events. Shared ground: both traditions read the questions as building toward the claim that disaster has a cause.

verses.text: Does the trumpet alarm sound in a city, without the people being afraid? Does evil happen to a city, and the LORD hasn’t done it?
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos asks, “Does evil happen to a city, and the LORD hasn’t done it?” Arminian readers see God as Lord over calamity.

They often describe his role as permitting or directing disaster in judgment, not causing moral evil.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Evil” here means calamity or disaster, not moral wrong. Compare Isaiah 45:7. On God and evil, see the box at Judges 9:23.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over disaster. Shared ground: God is not the author of sin.

verses.text: Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.”

Arminian readers see God graciously warning before judgment, giving people time to turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse explains why Amos speaks: God reveals his plans through his prophets.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in revealing his purposes. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s grace in giving warning before he acts.

verses.text: The lion has roared. Who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken. Who can but prophesy?
verses.arminianNotes:
“The lion has roared. Who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken. Who can but prophesy?” Arminian readers see the prophet compelled by God’s word.

Amos’s speaking is the natural result of God’s speaking.
verses.reformedNotes:
The questions reach their conclusion: God has spoken, so the prophet must speak (compare 7:14–15).

Reformed readers see God’s call as irresistible for the prophet. Shared ground: both traditions read this as the prophet’s call driven by God’s word.
